title: DNS in depth
scopeHtml:
Scope: recursive vs authoritative resolvers, record types, TTL and caching, DNS failures, GeoDNS.

Scope: recursive vs authoritative resolvers, record types, TTL and caching, DNS failures, GeoDNS.

notes.title: What DNS does
notes.html:
DNS (Domain Name System) turns a name like api.shop.com into an IP address like 203.0.113.10. Computers route by IP; humans remember names. DNS is a giant, distributed, cached phone book.

It is hierarchical: the root (.) knows who runs .com; the .com servers know who runs shop.com; shop.com's own servers know the address of api.shop.com. Nobody holds the whole book.

Worked example. Cold lookup of api.shop.com: resolver asks a root (about 1 ms away, anycast), gets "ask the .com servers" (referral), asks .com (about 10 ms), gets "ask ns1.shop.com", asks that (about 20 ms) and gets the A record. Total about 30 to 60 ms uncached. The next 300 seconds it answers from cache in under 1 ms.

Industry examples. There are 13 root server identities (A to M) but hundreds of anycast instances worldwide. Cloudflare 1.1.1.1, Google 8.8.8.8 and Quad9 9.9.9.9 are public recursive resolvers. Route 53, Cloudflare DNS and NS1 are popular authoritative hosts.

Everyday analogy. Asking a librarian for a book: she points you to the right floor, then the right shelf, then the right book. After the first time she remembers where it is.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying DNS is "one server". It is a hierarchy plus caches.
  • Forgetting that the first lookup is slow and almost everything after is cached.
  • Thinking DNS is only UDP. Large answers and zone transfers use TCP; DNS over TLS/HTTPS also exist.

notes.title: Recursive vs authoritative
notes.html:
Authoritative servers hold the truth for a zone and answer only about their own domains. Recursive resolvers do the legwork for clients: they chase the hierarchy and cache what they learn.

  • Stub resolver: tiny code in your OS or app. It asks one recursive resolver and trusts it.
  • Recursive resolver (recursor): run by your ISP, company, or a public provider. Asks roots, TLDs, authoritative servers, caches results.
  • Authoritative: runs for the domain owner. Gives answers with the aa flag set. Does not chase anything for others.
  • Iterative query: server replies "I do not know, ask X" (a referral). Recursive query: server promises the final answer or an error.

Decision gravity. Using a public resolver (8.8.8.8) versus the ISP one is fully reversible (one setting). Choosing an authoritative DNS provider is almost reversible but the nameserver change at the registrar has a TTL on its NS records (often 48 h), so migration is slow. Run two providers (multi-provider NS) to survive a provider outage; the 2016 Dyn DDoS took down Twitter, Netflix and GitHub for hours for sites that relied on a single provider.

Tool sample.

$ dig +trace api.shop.com
.                 518400 IN NS a.root-servers.net.
com.              172800 IN NS a.gtld-servers.net.
shop.com.         172800 IN NS ns1.dnsprov.net.
api.shop.com.        300 IN A  203.0.113.10

Everyday analogy. A recursive resolver is a travel agent who calls hotels for you; an authoritative server is the hotel front desk that only knows its own rooms.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up "recursive" (a service to clients) with "recursion available" on an authoritative server (should be off; open recursors get abused for DDoS amplification).
  • Believing authoritative servers cache. They answer from their zone data.

notes.title: Record types
notes.html:
Each DNS record has a name, type, TTL and data. The ones every senior must know:

Type Meaning Example
A Name to IPv4 api A 203.0.113.10
AAAA Name to IPv6 api AAAA 2001:db8::10
CNAME Alias to another name www CNAME shop.com.
NS Who is authoritative shop.com NS ns1.dnsprov.net.
MX Mail servers with priority MX 10 mail.shop.com.
TXT Free text: SPF, DKIM, domain verification "v=spf1 include:_spf.google.com ~all"
SRV Host and port for a service _sip._tcp SRV 10 5 5060 sip.shop.com.
PTR Reverse: IP to name 10.113.0.203.in-addr.arpa PTR api.shop.com.
SOA Zone metadata, serial, timers one per zone
CAA Which CAs may issue certificates 0 issue "letsencrypt.org"

CNAME rules. A CNAME cannot coexist with other records on the same name, so it cannot sit at the zone apex (shop.com itself, which must have SOA and NS). Providers invent "ALIAS" or "ANAME" (Route 53 alias, Cloudflare CNAME flattening) that resolve on the server side and return A records.

Worked example. Pointing shop.com at an AWS ALB (which has a changing set of IPs): use a Route 53 alias A record, not a hard-coded IP and not a CNAME. Pointing www.shop.com at a CDN: CNAME to shop.cdn.net. is fine.

Industry examples. Email deliverability (Gmail, Yahoo) now expects SPF, DKIM and DMARC TXT records. Kubernetes uses SRV and A records internally (svc.namespace.svc.cluster.local).

Everyday analogy. A contact card: A is the street address, CNAME is "also known as", MX is the mailroom, TXT is notes stuck on the card.

Common interview traps.

  • CNAME at the apex.
  • A CNAME chain that is five long; each hop is another lookup.
  • Forgetting TXT/SPF limits (10 DNS lookups in SPF).

notes.title: TTL and caching
notes.html:
TTL (time to live) is how many seconds a resolver may keep an answer before asking again. It is the single dial trading speed and load against freshness.

Caches stack: browser (about 1 min in Chrome), OS, router, ISP/public recursor, sometimes app libraries (Java networkaddress.cache.ttl, default 30 s, or forever with a security manager). Each respects its own idea of TTL, and some ignore low values.

Worked example (planned migration). Today api.shop.com A 1.1.1.1 TTL 86400. You want to move to 2.2.2.2 on Saturday. On Thursday lower TTL to 60. Wait at least the old TTL (24 h). Change the record Saturday. Within ~1 minute nearly everyone moves. Afterwards raise TTL back to 3600 to cut query load. If you skip the first step, some users see the old server for up to 24 h.

Negative caching. "This name does not exist" (NXDOMAIN) is cached for the SOA minimum field, often 300 to 3600 s. If you query a name before creating it, you may see NXDOMAIN long after creating it.

Decision gravity. TTL is reversible but its effect is delayed by the old TTL, so decide it before you need it. Typical choices: 300 s for services you may fail over, 3600 s to 86400 s for stable records (MX, NS). Very low TTLs (5 s) multiply query cost (Route 53 bills per million queries) and hurt latency.

Tool sample.

$ dig api.shop.com +noall +answer
api.shop.com.  247 IN A 203.0.113.10   # 247 s left in this resolver's cache

Everyday analogy. Writing a friend's number on a sticky note with an expiry date. Long expiry: fewer calls to the directory, but a stale number if they move.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming a changed record is live instantly.
  • Lowering TTL only at the moment of migration.
  • JVM or long-lived connection pools holding a stale IP forever.

notes.title: Common DNS failures
notes.html:
Know the symptoms and the first command for each.

Symptom Likely cause First check
NXDOMAIN Name missing, typo, record not yet propagated, negative cache dig name and ask the authoritative directly
SERVFAIL Authoritative down, broken DNSSEC, lame delegation dig +trace, dig +cd
Timeout UDP blocked, resolver down, packet loss dig @8.8.8.8 name versus local resolver
Wrong/old IP TTL not expired, split-horizon mismatch dig +short against several resolvers
Works on laptop, fails in container Container uses different resolver (/etc/resolv.conf) cat /etc/resolv.conf inside it
Slow app, DNS 5 s stalls search domains and ndots:5 in Kubernetes cause many failed lookups ndots setting, use FQDN with trailing dot

Real incident pattern. A Kubernetes pod resolves api.shop.com and CoreDNS gets 5 queries (api.shop.com.default.svc.cluster.local, ...) before the real one. Under load CoreDNS drops UDP packets (conntrack race), and the app sees random 5 s stalls (glibc retry timeout). Metric: coredns_dns_request_duration_seconds p99 and node_nf_conntrack_stat_insert_failed. Fix: NodeLocal DNSCache, lower ndots, FQDN with trailing dot.

Another: Facebook outage of October 2021. A BGP change withdrew routes to its authoritative DNS servers; the servers then took themselves offline because they could not reach the data centres. The whole world's resolvers got timeouts for facebook.com, and the retry storm loaded other resolvers.

Everyday analogy. A phone book that is missing a page (NXDOMAIN), whose publisher is closed (SERVFAIL), or where you cannot even reach the phone (timeout).

Common interview traps.

  • Mistaking NXDOMAIN (answer: no) for SERVFAIL (answer: I could not find out).
  • Forgetting that DNS failures look like "the app is slow", not "DNS is down".
  • Not mentioning retries and timeout settings (resolv.conf timeout:5 attempts:2).

notes.title: GeoDNS and traffic steering
notes.html:
GeoDNS gives different answers to different users, based on where the query appears to come from. It is the oldest way to send European users to Frankfurt and Indian users to Mumbai.

Variants:

  • Geolocation routing: by resolver IP (or EDNS Client Subnet, a hint of the client's real subnet).
  • Latency-based: Route 53 picks the region with the lowest measured latency.
  • Weighted: 90% old, 10% new for canaries.
  • Failover: health checks remove a dead target (record TTL 30 to 60 s).
  • Anycast: the same IP is announced from many places; BGP picks the nearest (used by Cloudflare, root servers).

Worked example. Failover with TTL 60 and health check interval 10 s, 3 failures: detection 30 s plus up to 60 s of cache = up to 90 s of bad traffic. Browsers and apps that cache longer (or reuse connections) take longer. For faster failover use anycast or an L4/L7 global load balancer.

Industry examples. Netflix and CDNs (Akamai historically) steer by DNS; AWS Global Accelerator and Cloudflare use anycast IPs instead; Google uses both anycast and its own front ends.

Decision gravity. GeoDNS is easy to add and remove (reversible). Relying on DNS failover as your only HA is risky because the clients' cache is out of your control. A user using a far-away public resolver gets the resolver's region unless ECS is passed.

Everyday analogy. A directory operator who gives you the number of the shop branch closest to where you are calling from.

Common interview traps.

  • Believing DNS failover is instant.
  • Forgetting that the resolver location, not the user's, is what GeoDNS sees without ECS.
  • Using GeoDNS for stateful data routing without thinking about replication.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• DNS is a hierarchy (root, TLD, authoritative) plus layers of caches; stub asks recursor, recursor iterates.
  • Authoritative servers own zones; recursors cache. Run two authoritative providers for resilience.
  • Know A, AAAA, CNAME (no apex), NS, MX, TXT, SRV, PTR, SOA, CAA; use ALIAS/flattening at the apex.
  • TTL is a delayed dial: lower it before migrations; negative answers are cached too.
  • Debug with dig, dig +trace, comparing resolvers; NXDOMAIN is "no", SERVFAIL is "could not find out".
  • GeoDNS, weighted, failover and anycast steer traffic; DNS failover is limited by client caches (60 to 90 s typical).

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between a recursive resolver and an authoritative name server?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Most DNS debugging starts by knowing which role you are talking to.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An authoritative server holds the actual records for a zone and answers with the final truth for it. A recursive resolver works on behalf of clients: it walks the hierarchy (root, TLD, authoritative), caches results, and returns the answer. Clients talk to recursive resolvers, resolvers talk to authoritative servers.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
For api.example.com, a cold resolver asks a root server (gets the .com NS), asks a .com server (gets example.com's NS), then asks example.com's authoritative server (gets the A record). Each step may be cached according to TTL. Authoritative answers carry the aa flag; cached answers from a resolver do not. Stub resolvers in your OS just forward to a configured recursive resolver.

client -> stub -> recursive resolver -> root -> .com TLD -> example.com NS
                         ^ caches                 (referrals, then final answer)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
dig +trace api.example.com          # follow the walk yourself
dig @ns1.example.com api.example.com +norecurse   # ask authoritative directly; look for 'aa'

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking the registrar's nameserver and the recursive resolver are the same thing.
  • Changing a record at the authoritative server and testing through a cached resolver.
  • Forgetting glue records when the NS is inside the zone it serves.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does the aa flag mean? -> Answer comes straight from an authoritative server.
  2. What is glue? -> A/AAAA of an NS given at the parent to avoid circular lookup.
  3. Who decides how long a resolver caches? -> The record's TTL, bounded by resolver policy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average describes the walk. Senior adds caching layers (stub, OS, resolver, browser), negative caching and how to query each layer in isolation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team verified a DNS change with dig against 8.8.8.8 and declared success while their corporate resolver still served the old answer.

questions.promptHtml: Explain A, AAAA, CNAME, NS, MX, TXT and SRV records. Which restrictions on CNAME matter?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: CNAME-at-apex and MX confusion cause real outages.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A/AAAA map a name to IPv4/IPv6. CNAME makes a name an alias of another name. NS delegates a zone. MX routes mail. TXT holds arbitrary text (SPF, verification). SRV gives host, port, priority and weight for a service. A CNAME cannot coexist with other records at the same name, so it cannot sit at the zone apex.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The apex (example.com) must have SOA and NS records, so a CNAME there would conflict. Providers solve it with ALIAS/ANAME (flattening at the authoritative side, answering with A records). A CNAME chain adds lookups and latency; resolvers follow it. MX must point to a name with an A/AAAA, not a CNAME. SRV is used by Kubernetes, SIP and others.

Type Value
A / AAAA IP address
CNAME canonical name
NS name server host
MX priority + mail host
TXT text (SPF, DKIM)
SRV priority weight port target

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Putting a CNAME at the apex and breaking MX/NS.
  • Long CNAME chains that multiply TTL effects and failures.
  • Assuming TTL of the alias equals the target's TTL; each record has its own.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you point apex to a load balancer hostname? -> ALIAS/ANAME or CNAME flattening.
  2. What is a PTR record? -> Reverse lookup, IP to name in in-addr.arpa.
  3. Why does SPF live in TXT? -> It was a generic record; a separate SPF type was deprecated.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average lists types. Senior knows apex restrictions, flattening, chain cost and TTL interaction.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Adding a CNAME at the apex for a CDN silently killed company email because MX records were shadowed.

questions.promptHtml: What is DNS TTL and how does it affect a planned migration?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Checks whether you plan changes around cache expiry.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: TTL is how many seconds a resolver may cache an answer. Before migrating, I lower the TTL (say from 24 h to 60 s) at least one old-TTL period ahead, make the change, watch traffic drain, then raise TTL again. Lowering it at the time of the change is too late because caches hold the old long TTL.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A resolver stores the record with its TTL counting down; the answer returned to a client shows the remaining TTL. Some resolvers, browsers and JVMs ignore or override TTL (the JVM historically cached forever with a security manager; check networkaddress.cache.ttl). Low TTLs raise query volume and expose you to authoritative outages sooner. Negative answers (NXDOMAIN) are cached for the SOA's minimum/negative TTL.

T-24h: TTL 86400 -> 60
T-0 : change IP
T+1h: traffic on old IP ~0 (except TTL violators)
T+1d: raise TTL to 3600

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Lowering TTL at the moment of change.
  • Expecting instant failover with 300 s TTL (clients and apps add their own caching).
  • Forgetting negative caching after creating a record that previously did not exist.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why not always use TTL 5? -> Query load, latency, and dependency on DNS availability.
  2. How does a JVM service cache? -> networkaddress.cache.ttl and negative.ttl security properties; verify defaults.
  3. What is serve-stale? -> Resolver may return expired data when authoritative is unreachable (RFC 8767).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average says "wait for TTL". Senior pre-lowers TTL, knows TTL violators, and plans rollback by keeping the old endpoint alive.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A cutover assumed 60 s TTL, but a legacy client library cached DNS for 30 minutes and kept hitting the decommissioned IP.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through everything that happens from typing a hostname in a program to getting an IP, including the caches.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests depth: caches, config files, protocols, failure points.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The app calls getaddrinfo; libc checks /etc/hosts and nsswitch order, then asks the stub/system resolver (maybe systemd-resolved or a local cache), which asks the configured recursive resolver over UDP/53 (TCP on truncation). The resolver checks its cache, otherwise walks root, TLD, authoritative. The answer returns up the chain, each layer caching by TTL.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layers: application cache (JVM, browser, Go's none by default), OS resolver/cache, search domains and ndots (in Kubernetes ndots:5 makes api try several suffixes before the real name, multiplying queries), recursive resolver, authoritative. Both A and AAAA are queried in parallel; a dropped AAAA response can cause a 5 s timeout. UDP responses over 512 B (or EDNS0 buffer size) are truncated (TC bit) and retried over TCP. DNSSEC, DoT, DoH change transport and validation.

app -> getaddrinfo -> /etc/hosts -> stub (127.0.0.53) -> resolver -> root/TLD/auth

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
cat /etc/resolv.conf          # nameserver, search, options ndots
getent hosts api.example.com  # same path as apps (nsswitch)
dig api.example.com           # bypasses nsswitch

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Using dig to debug an app problem when the app uses getaddrinfo with a different path.
  • Ignoring search domains and ndots.
  • Forgetting AAAA lookups.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why can a Kubernetes pod make 5+ queries for one name? -> ndots:5 plus search list.
  2. When does DNS use TCP? -> Truncation, zone transfers, large DNSSEC responses, DoT.
  3. What is EDNS0? -> Extension allowing UDP payloads above 512 B.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "browser asks DNS". Senior knows nsswitch, ndots, parallel A/AAAA and where timeouts come from.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Latency in a Kubernetes service dropped by 40 ms p50 after using fully qualified names with a trailing dot.

questions.contextHtml:
You moved a payments API from 198.51.100.10 to a new load balancer 203.0.113.50 at 02:00. TTL was 300 s (lowered from 3600 the day before, 20 hours earlier). At 03:00 the old servers still receive 15% of traffic. At 06:00 still 4%. You planned to decommission the old box at 03:00. Clients are mobile apps and a few partner servers. Red herring: Route 53 shows the new record correct and dig @8.8.8.8 returns the new IP.

$ dig +short api.pay.example.com @1.1.1.1
203.0.113.50
old LB access log source mix: 60% Java partner servers, 40% Android app
questions.promptHtml: Why is traffic still hitting the old IP and what do you do?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "DNS propagation takes time," then waits, or decommissions anyway.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which clients still hit the old IP? Do they honor TTL? Do any hardcode the IP? Any long-lived connections?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Keep the old endpoint serving (or reverse-proxy it to the new one); do not decommission.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Clients with their own DNS cache ignoring TTL (JVM with infinite cache or HTTP pool keeping connections); long-lived keep-alive connections to old IP; hardcoded IPs or partner allow-lists; resolvers violating TTL.
  4. How I'd verify each: Group old-LB logs by User-Agent and source; check JVM networkaddress.cache.ttl; look at connection age in ss -ti; ask partners.
  5. Root cause: DNS TTL only controls resolver caching; Java partners cached the lookup indefinitely and Android keep-alive pools reused existing sockets.
  6. Fix: Short term: proxy old IP to new LB, contact partners to restart or fix cache settings. Long term: send Connection: close/GOAWAY periodically, document client DNS settings.
  7. Prevention: Migration checklist: client survey, TTL lowering well in advance, keep old path for 2x max TTL, track traffic per old IP.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not cut the old IP off on schedule; running two endpoints costs money but is cheaper than failed payments.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Partner allow-lists new IPs? -> Needs coordination; consider keeping IPs stable (anycast/elastic IPs).
  • How to avoid the problem? -> Use stable VIP/anycast and change backends behind it.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a partner's JVM cached the old IP for 11 days until a scheduled restart; the old LB had been terminated and the integration failed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: waits and decommissions.
  • Hire: finds client caching/keep-alive and keeps old path.
  • Strong hire: segments traffic, adds server-side drain, prevention checklist.

questions.contextHtml:
A service on Linux (glibc) sometimes takes exactly 5 seconds for its first call to a downstream API; subsequent calls are fast. About 1 in 200 lookups. The VPC resolver is healthy per the cloud provider. Strace of the slow call:

sendto(5, "...api.internal.example.com A...", ...)
sendto(5, "...api.internal.example.com AAAA...", ...)
recvfrom(5, ... A answer ...)
poll([{fd=5, events=POLLIN}], 1, 5000) = 0 (Timeout)
sendto(5, ...AAAA again...)   # after 5s

Red herring: CPU and network look normal.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the timeout" or blame the application code.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is it first call only? Is it A or AAAA that times out? Any conntrack or firewall in the path?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Set options single-request-reopen or timeout:1 attempts:3 in /etc/resolv.conf; cache lookups app-side.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: A and AAAA sent in parallel from the same socket/port; a conntrack/SNAT race drops one reply; resolver drops AAAA; packet loss; search domain expansion.
  4. How I'd verify each: tcpdump -ni any port 53 showing both queries with same source port and one missing reply; conntrack -S for insert_failed; dig AAAA directly.
  5. Root cause: glibc sends A and AAAA in parallel on the same 5-tuple; a Linux conntrack race can drop one reply; glibc waits the default 5 s timeout before retrying.
  6. Fix: single-request-reopen/single-request options, or a local caching resolver (NodeLocal DNSCache, dnsmasq), UDP conntrack bypass, kernel patch level update.
  7. Prevention: Alert on conntrack insert_failed, monitor DNS latency percentiles, keep a node-level cache.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not disable IPv6 broadly; not just lower timeout without understanding.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Alpine/musl image? -> musl has different resolver behavior (parallel, no search ordering); verify.
  • Why does it hit 1 in 200? -> A race requiring simultaneous packets on the same flow.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a mysterious 5 s p99 on a Kubernetes cluster disappeared after deploying a node-local DNS cache.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: bumps timeouts.
  • Hire: ties it to A/AAAA and resolver timeout.
  • Strong hire: conntrack race, local cache, metrics.

questions.contextHtml: Last night your authoritative DNS provider had a 90-minute outage. Your site (TTL 60 s on A records, 300 s on NS from registrar) went fully dark after about 5 minutes, even though your servers were healthy. A competitor with TTL 3600 stayed partly reachable. Status page: the provider's anycast network was hit by a DDoS. You get to present the post-incident review. Traffic: 40k req/s, SLO 99.95%.
questions.promptHtml: What do you conclude, and what changes do you propose?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Choose a better provider," with nothing about TTL trade-offs, redundancy, or serve-stale.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Was the zone on a single provider? Any NS at another provider? Do our own resolvers serve stale?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (retrospective) Activate secondary provider or increase TTL during the incident if still possible.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Single-provider dependency; short TTL means caches expire during the outage; no serve-stale on major resolvers; health-check failover itself needs DNS.
  4. How I'd verify each: Review resolver logs/SERVFAIL rates, timeline vs TTL expiry, NS records at the registrar, provider post-mortem.
  5. Root cause: DNS is a hard dependency: with TTL 60, caches expired a minute in and nothing could refill them. Short TTL buys agility at the cost of outage tolerance.
  6. Fix: Multi-provider authoritative setup (two vendors, zone sync via IaC/AXFR), moderate TTL (300-3600 s) for stable records and low TTL only where failover needs it, plan for DNSSEC with multiple signers, rehearsed runbook.
  7. Prevention: Synthetic probes from several resolvers, game day that blocks one provider, registrar-level NS monitoring.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not set everything to 1 day (slows failover); multi-provider loses provider-specific features (geo, weighted) and requires sync discipline.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Does serve-stale save you? -> Only if resolvers implement it; don't rely on it.
  • Registrar outage? -> Consider registry lock and a second registrar account for DR plans.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: after a similar event, a company discovered both "redundant" NS records were the same vendor's different clusters.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames vendor.
  • Hire: multi-provider and TTL analysis.
  • Strong hire: quantifies TTL expiry timeline, handles feature parity and rehearsals.

questions.promptHtml: How does GeoDNS or latency-based DNS routing work, and what are its limits?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Many candidates assume DNS knows where the user is.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: The authoritative server returns different answers based on where the query seems to come from. But it sees the recursive resolver's IP, not the user's, unless EDNS Client Subnet (ECS) is passed. So steering is only as good as the resolver location and cached for the TTL.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The authoritative checks the source IP (or ECS prefix, typically /24) against a geo or latency database and picks the nearest endpoint, possibly with health checks. Problems: public resolvers (8.8.8.8, 1.1.1.1) are anycast so their egress may be far from the user; some resolvers don't send ECS for privacy (Cloudflare doesn't); caches keyed by ECS fragment hit rates; TTL limits failover speed; geo databases go stale. Anycast routing at the IP layer (same IP announced in many places) is an alternative or complement that moves steering into BGP and fails over faster.

Method Decides by Failover speed
GeoDNS resolver/ECS location TTL-bound
Latency DNS measured latency to region TTL-bound
Anycast BGP shortest path seconds

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming user location equals resolver location.
  • Forgetting that TTL limits health-check failover.
  • Not testing from the target regions.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is ECS? -> Resolver includes the client subnet so authoritative can geolocate better.
  2. Why does Cloudflare 1.1.1.1 not send ECS? -> Privacy; relies on anycast presence.
  3. How would you fail a region over? -> Health check removes it from answers; low TTL; plus app-level retry.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average: "returns IP closest to user". Senior: resolver vs user, ECS, TTL-bound failover, mixing with anycast.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Corporate users in Singapore routed through a US-based resolver got US endpoints until ECS was enabled.

questions.promptHtml: Explain NXDOMAIN, SERVFAIL, REFUSED and timeouts. What does each tell you?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Quick triage skill during outages.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: NXDOMAIN: the name doesn't exist (authoritative said so). SERVFAIL: the resolver couldn't get a valid answer (upstream failure, DNSSEC validation failure, lame delegation). REFUSED: the server won't answer you (ACL/recursion off). Timeout: nothing came back (network, firewall, dead server). Each points to a different layer.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
NXDOMAIN gets negative-cached per the SOA minimum; a typo or race on record creation can linger. SERVFAIL is ambiguous: use dig +cd (checking disabled) to see if DNSSEC validation is the cause, or query authoritatives directly. Lame delegation: parent lists an NS that is not authoritative for the zone. REFUSED often arises when you query an authoritative with recursion or from a disallowed IP. NOERROR with empty answer ("NODATA") means the name exists but not that type, such as AAAA missing.

dig example.com +cd        # bypass DNSSEC validation
dig @ns1.example.com example.com SOA +norecurse
dig +tcp example.com       # test TCP path / truncation

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Treating NODATA as NXDOMAIN.
  • Not checking every NS: one lame server causes intermittent failures.
  • Forgetting an expired DNSSEC signature produces SERVFAIL only for validating resolvers.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why does one in four lookups fail? -> One of four NS is broken/lame; resolvers round-robin.
  2. Why would only 8.8.8.8 users fail? -> DNSSEC validation (broken DS or signature).
  3. How long is NXDOMAIN cached? -> SOA negative TTL (min of SOA minimum and TTL).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: Average maps codes to words. Senior uses +cd, +norecurse per NS and thinks through negative caching.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An expired RRSIG took a domain offline for validating resolvers only, so internal tests passed.

questions.contextHtml:
After the marketing team pointed example.com (apex) to a SaaS landing page using a CNAME in the DNS UI (the UI allowed it), outbound mail from the company starts bouncing with "no MX for example.com" for some recipients, and Google Search Console verification via TXT also fails. Website works. DNS provider is a small vendor. dig example.com MX returns different results from different resolvers.

$ dig example.com CNAME +short
landing.saas-vendor.io.
$ dig example.com MX +short
(empty on some resolvers; old MX on others)
questions.promptHtml: What happened and how do you fix it without breaking the website?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Restores MX records and leaves CNAME, assuming both can coexist.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Exactly what records exist at the apex now? Does the provider offer ALIAS/ANAME? What's the TTL?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remove the CNAME at the apex and replace with A records provided by the SaaS vendor, or use ALIAS; restore MX/TXT.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: CNAME coexisting with MX/TXT/NS/SOA violates RFC; some resolvers return only the CNAME and ignore other data; caching inconsistent; MX target problem.
  4. How I'd verify each: dig @authoritative example.com ANY/each type; compare across resolvers; check zone export.
  5. Root cause: A CNAME means "all data for this name is at the target", so other records at that name are invalid; behavior is undefined and resolver-dependent, hence inconsistent results.
  6. Fix: Use A/AAAA with vendor IPs, or the provider's CNAME flattening/ALIAS; redirect example.com to www (CNAME there) at the HTTP layer.
  7. Prevention: Zone linting in CI (e.g. octoDNS/dnscontrol validate), change review, provider with RFC checks.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rely on vendor IPs staying fixed without a monitoring plan; ALIAS adds provider lock-in.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why is www safe for CNAME? -> No required apex records exist there.
  • Can MX target be a CNAME? -> RFC says no; some MTAs tolerate.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a startup lost inbound email for hours after a DNS UI change; flattening records fixed it.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: keeps both.
  • Hire: explains CNAME exclusivity and fixes.
  • Strong hire: ALIAS/flattening and zone linting.

questions.contextHtml:
A cluster with 3 CoreDNS pods handles 6k QPS. Traffic is growing 10x next quarter. Today p99 DNS latency is 8 ms, but CoreDNS CPU is 70% and shows many NXDOMAIN answers.

coredns_dns_responses_total{rcode="NXDOMAIN"}  72%
sample query log:
  api.payments.svc.cluster.local.default.svc.cluster.local  NXDOMAIN
  api.payments.svc.cluster.local.svc.cluster.local          NXDOMAIN
  api.payments.svc.cluster.local.                           NOERROR

Pods' resolv.conf has ndots:5. Red herring: the upstream resolver latency is flat.
questions.promptHtml: Why is the load so high and how do you scale it to 60k QPS?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add more CoreDNS replicas" only.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which clients create most queries? Do they use FQDN? Are there short-lived pods doing many lookups? What are cache hit rates?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Scale CoreDNS replicas and raise cache TTL for cluster.local.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: ndots:5 expansion multiplies queries 3-5x; A+AAAA doubling; no client-side caching; conntrack/UDP DNAT limits; upstream external queries uncached.
  4. How I'd verify each: CoreDNS log plugin sampling; Prometheus cache hit/miss; conntrack -S; per-pod query counts.
  5. Root cause: Names with fewer than 5 dots are tried against each search suffix first, so each lookup becomes 4-6 queries, most NXDOMAIN.
  6. Fix: Use trailing-dot FQDNs or set dnsConfig: ndots: 2 for chatty pods; deploy NodeLocal DNSCache (per-node cache, TCP to upstream, avoids conntrack); autoscale CoreDNS (cluster-proportional-autoscaler); enable autopath if appropriate.
  7. Prevention: Load test DNS at 3x; dashboard QPS per namespace; lint config for FQDN usage.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: ndots:1 may break short service names; autopath adds CoreDNS memory and requires pod identification; don't just inflate replicas as UDP conntrack stays a bottleneck.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Why does NodeLocal help conntrack? -> Pod to node-local cache avoids DNAT; the cache uses TCP upstream.
  • Lookups of external hosts? -> Still go through search list unless FQDN.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: batch job pods generating 20k QPS of NXDOMAIN knocked cluster DNS over; adding a trailing dot to one config key cut it by 80%.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: replicas only.
  • Hire: identifies ndots and NodeLocal.
  • Strong hire: quantifies multiplier, conntrack, autoscaler and tests.

questions.contextHtml: You run active-active in us-east and eu-west serving 25k req/s each. Product wants "automatic failover within 30 seconds if a region dies" using DNS health checks. You have TTL 30 s records with health checks every 10 s and 3 consecutive failures to mark unhealthy. Clients include browsers, mobile SDKs with their own DNS caching, and partners with connection pools.
questions.promptHtml: Can DNS meet this requirement? What would you build?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Yes, TTL is 30 s so failover is 30 s."

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is 30 s a hard SLO? Which clients? Is state replicated? What's the cost of partial failure?
  2. Immediate mitigation: N/A; design.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Detection time (10 s x 3 = 30 s) + TTL (30 s) + client caches + keep-alive = 60-120+ s; DNS cannot reach partner pools; browsers retry other IPs if multiple A records.
  4. How I'd verify each: Failure drills: block a region and measure time until traffic drains per client type; check client DNS caching behavior.
  5. Root cause: DNS-based failover is bounded by detection + TTL + client caching; it's best-effort and typically 1-5 min tail.
  6. Fix: Use anycast or a global load balancer for fast IP-level steering; return multiple A records so clients retry; client SDK retries with a regional fallback endpoint list; reduce detection to 3 x 5 s; make data layer region-tolerant.
  7. Prevention: Quarterly game days, SLO measuring failover time, runbook for manual weight shift.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: TTL 5 s raises query cost and DNS dependence; don't promise 30 s via DNS alone; avoid flapping with hysteresis.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Split-brain health checks? -> Check from multiple vantage points and require quorum.
  • Failback? -> Slow, weighted ramp to avoid thundering herd.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a failover test showed 90% moved in 45 s but 3% of clients took 20 minutes because of a pinned HTTP/2 connection.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: equates TTL with failover.
  • Hire: sums detection + TTL + client caches.
  • Strong hire: anycast/GLB design, drills and flapping control.

questions.contextHtml:
A Java 17 service resolves a backend through DNS with weights shifted by a service registry that updates A records with TTL 30 s. During a blue/green cut, 100% of the traffic should shift within a minute, but the service keeps hitting blue for hours. A teammate shows the setup:

// startup
java.security.Security.setProperty("networkaddress.cache.ttl", "-1");
// client
static final InetAddress BACKEND = InetAddress.getByName("backend.internal.example.com");
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newHttpClient();
URI uri = URI.create("http://" + BACKEND.getHostAddress() + ":8080/v1/items");

Red herring: the DNS records do update correctly.
questions.promptHtml: Find all the bugs and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Only notices the cache property.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is a security manager used (changes JVM default)? Is a proxy/sidecar in the path? Does the HTTP client pool connections?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Restart pods to re-resolve; set a TTL via property.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) ttl=-1 caches forever; (b) address resolved once into a static final, ignoring DNS afterwards; (c) IP literal in URI bypasses DNS completely; (d) HTTP keep-alive keeps old connections.
  4. How I'd verify each: Heap/thread inspection; log resolved address per request; ss -tn for established connection age; tcpdump port 53 showing zero DNS queries.
  5. Root cause: DNS is resolved exactly once at class load and pinned as an IP, so TTL is irrelevant.
  6. Fix: Remove the static; use the hostname in the URI; set networkaddress.cache.ttl=30 (and negative.ttl=5); configure client connection max age (or Connection: close periodically).
  7. Prevention: Lint against resolving hosts at static init; integration test that flips DNS and asserts traffic moves; document the JVM DNS properties.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Too-low cache TTL increases lookups and ties availability to DNS; a service mesh may be better for weighted shifts.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Default JVM cache? -> Usually 30 s without a security manager; verify per JDK.
  • Does Netty/gRPC re-resolve? -> gRPC name resolvers re-resolve on connection failure or on schedule; check config.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a cutover ran 3 days on the old fleet because one library cached resolved IPs in a singleton.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: spots only the property.
  • Hire: finds static pin and IP literal.
  • Strong hire: includes keep-alive, tests, and mesh alternative.

questions.contextHtml:
At 09:10 customers using one ISP report your site resolves to an unknown IP serving a login look-alike page. Your authoritative zone is unchanged. Users on other ISPs are fine. The look-alike IP is in a hosting range in another country. Your zone is not DNSSEC-signed. TTL is 3600 s. Security asks for a response plan within 15 minutes.

$ dig @isp-resolver.example.net www.example.com +short
192.0.2.250
$ dig @ns1.example.com www.example.com +short
203.0.113.50
questions.promptHtml: What happened and what do you do now and after?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Change our DNS records," which does nothing since our zone is correct.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Do all names or one? Which resolver IPs? Is it only that ISP? Any TLS errors seen by users?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Contact the ISP resolver team, report the phishing IP to its host, publish customer advisory; HSTS and valid TLS limit damage; consider takedown.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: Resolver cache poisoning; compromised resolver or upstream; BGP hijack of resolver or our prefix (would affect IPs, not DNS answers); registrar/NS tampering (ruled out by authoritative check).
  4. How I'd verify each: Compare answers across resolvers and authoritative; check TTL remaining on the bad answer; check dig +trace; confirm whether the fake page has a valid cert.
  5. Root cause: The ISP resolver holds a forged answer for up to the TTL; our authoritative data are right.
  6. Fix: ISP flushes its cache and patches; we sign the zone with DNSSEC so validating resolvers reject forgeries; keep TLS with HSTS preload so a fake IP can't present a valid cert.
  7. Prevention: DNSSEC with managed key rollover, CAA records, certificate transparency monitoring, synthetic DNS checks from major ISPs.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: DNSSEC adds operational risk (expired signatures cause outages) and doesn't protect clients using non-validating resolvers; don't lower TTL as a fix since poisoned entries respect the poisoner's TTL.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Would DoH help users? -> Moves trust to the DoH provider; avoids ISP tampering.
  • Why TLS matters here? -> The attacker can't get a trusted cert for your domain, so users see warnings.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a small ISP's resolver was poisoned for a bank brand; the registered CAA and HSTS preload limited credentials stolen to users clicking through warnings.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: edits own zone.
  • Hire: diagnoses resolver-level poisoning, escalates to ISP.
  • Strong hire: DNSSEC, HSTS/CAA, comms plan and trade-offs.
